time.desc: A group of content creators on the short video platform sued in federal court to block a law that requires the platform's parent company to divest it within a time limit or be banned nationwide, claiming that it infringes on their constitutionally protected right to expression.
The Federal Court announced a fast-track trial timetable for legal cases challenging the "stripping or banning" law, clarifying key submission nodes and court arrangements.

The government submitted its first systemic defense document in related litigation, emphasizing that the risk of data and content manipulation still poses a national security threat and opposing the repeal of the law.

The federal government and consumer privacy watchdogs filed a civil lawsuit against the short video platform and its parent company, accusing it of long-term illegal collection of data on underage children and violation of privacy protection laws.
The short-form video platform formally filed a lawsuit in federal court challenging the "strip or ban" law, saying it was based on false facts and violated free speech protections.
The appeals court held the first oral argument on the platform's challenge to the "strip or ban" law, as the platform and the government battled over constitutionality and national security risks.
Several states and regions jointly sued the short video platform, accusing it of harming minors with addictive product designs and misleading the public about the effectiveness of safety measures.

A government ordered the closure of the short video platform's local corporate operating entity, citing the conclusion of a national security review. The platform said it would file a judicial challenge but the app would still be available to users.

The Court of Appeal ruled to uphold the "divest or ban" law and rejected the platform's unconstitutional claim. It made it clear that failure to complete the divestment would trigger a ban and there may be an extension window. The platform announced that it would continue to appeal to the Supreme Court.
The platform applied to the court for an emergency stay to prevent the impending ban from taking effect, and the government filed documents opposing the stay request.
The appeals court rejected the platform's request for a stay, refusing to halt the implementation of the "strip or ban" law pending review by the higher court.

The platform and its parent company filed an emergency petition with the Supreme Court to temporarily block the "strip or ban" law from taking effect as scheduled, while elected leaders said publicly they were studying the issue.

The platform announced restrictions on the dissemination of overseas recommendation streams by some foreign-affiliated media accounts and prohibited them from advertising outside their home countries.
The platform began to develop its own independent version of the core algorithm to isolate domestic user data and alleviate data security concerns.
A presidential candidate officially joined the short video platform and posted his first video. The number of followers on his account exceeded millions within two days.

The platform confirmed that its private messaging function was attacked by a zero-day vulnerability, resulting in the hacking of multiple brand and celebrity accounts, and said that it had taken blocking measures.

Intelligence officials publicly accused the platform in court documents for the first time of censoring overseas content and storing user data on offshore servers at the request of foreign governments.
